Self-Credit: Credit Assignment for Long-Horizon Agentic RL via Intra-group Rescaling

Fangcong Yin Affiliation: Meta    Ming Yin Affiliation: Meta Affiliation: Duke University    Tanvi Bhandarkar Affiliation: Meta    Aashu Singh Affiliation: Meta    Eryk Helenowski Affiliation: Meta    Shlok Kumar Mishra Affiliation: Meta    Saghar Hosseini Affiliation: Meta    Karthik Abinav Sankararaman Affiliation: Meta    Greg Durrett Affiliation: New York University    Dinkar Juyal Affiliation: Meta
Abstract

LLM agents are commonly trained with RLVR, but the sparse nature of typical RLVR rewards makes credit assignment challenging, especially for long-horizon tasks. We propose Self-Credit, an end-to-end agentic RL method that creates dense supervision signals from sparse outcome rewards using self-generated credit assignment via intra-group rescaling. Self-Credit builds on group-based RL with three components. First, during its rollouts, the policy model generates summaries with citations to earlier turns containing critical evidence, which serve as self-generated credit. Second, we refine this model-generated credit with intra-group rescaling, which compares cited actions across successful and failed rollouts for the same prompt. This approach uses group-level agreement and disagreement to remove undeserved credit and further emphasize credit assigned to critical actions. Third, advantage reweighting uses the rescaled credit weights to update the advantages of the cited turns. On BrowseComp-Plus, Self-Credit improves over the base models by 37.037.0 and 36.236.2 points on Qwen3 8B and 32B respectively, and outperforms the strongest agentic RL baselines by 8.58.5 and 5.65.6 points, respectively. Self-Credit also improves over the strongest baselines by 4.94.9 points on GAIA and 4.74.7 points on xBench-DeepSearch. Analyses show that self-generated credit provides useful signals for selecting critical actions, and that intra-group rescaling, especially on failed rollouts, is important across model scales.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are commonly used for agentic tasks, where they interact with environments and issue tool calls as actions. A principal challenge in building long-horizon agents is the nature of supervision: typically, models are trained via RLVR using only sparse rewards (Guo et al., 2025), as additional dense supervision is expensive to define and collect (Tao et al., 2025; Setlur et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025e). Recent work extends standard RLVR algorithms to provide credit assignment even when only sparse rewards are available, including approaches that use external judges (Zhang et al., 2026b; Zeng et al., 2025) and learned critics (Zhang et al., 2025d; Shi et al., 2026). However, these methods usually require additional supervision signals and often suffer from context growth in challenging long-horizon tasks (Sun et al., 2025).

Inspired by context management methods for LLM agents (Li et al., 2026b; Xie et al., 2026), we propose Self-Credit, a novel agentic RL method in which the policy LLM agent performs credit assignment through compaction using self-generated credit with intra-group rescaling. As illustrated in Figure 1, Self-Credit builds on a standard group-based RL algorithm with three components to create dense supervision signals from a single sparse outcome reward. First, we prompt the policy model to generate a summary with citations that identify earlier turns in the interaction history containing critical evidence for the agentic task. The summaries are used for compaction to compress the long context, and the citations serve as self-generated credit. Second, intra-group rescaling refines this credit by comparing cited actions across successful and failed rollouts for the same prompt. In particular, this rescaling uses agreement and disagreement across the entire rollout group to determine how to remove undeserved credit and further emphasize credit assigned to critical actions, grounding the credit weights in group-level statistics. Third, advantage reweighting uses the rescaled credit weights to selectively strengthen the advantages of tokens in model-cited turns to emphasize important behaviors in a long trajectory.

We evaluate Self-Credit on challenging long-horizon search and retrieval tasks, including multi-hop QA on BrowseComp-Plus and deep research on GAIA and xBench-DeepSearch. As shown in Figure 1, on BrowseComp-Plus, Self-Credit improves over the Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B base agents by 37.037.0 and 36.236.2 percentage points, respectively, and outperforms the strongest agentic RL baselines by 8.58.5 and 5.65.6 points, respectively. On deep research tasks, Self-Credit also outperforms the strongest evaluated baselines by 4.94.9 points on GAIA and 4.74.7 points on xBench-DeepSearch.

Ablations show that intra-group credit rescaling, especially downweighting repeated turns shared across failed rollouts, is important across model scales, and that using self-generated credit provides more effective credit assignment than the alternatives. Further analyses show that self-generated citations identify important actions related to gold answers, and that intra-group rescaling rules are applied selectively during training at a higher selection quality than baselines.

Our main contributions are as follows: (1) We introduce Self-Credit, an end-to-end RL algorithm for training long-horizon agents using self-generated summaries for turn-level credit assignment with intra-group rescaling. (2) We propose a novel intra-group credit rescaling method that refines self-generated credit using both successful and failed rollouts. (3) We show that Self-Credit outperforms strong agentic RL baselines on long-horizon agentic tasks across multiple models at different scales.

2 Preliminaries

Long-horizon agentic tasks. We formulate long-horizon tasks for LLM agents as follows. Given a query QQ, an LLM agent MθM_{\theta} interacts with an environment ℰ\mathcal{E} and answers QQ by taking a sequence of actions over TT interaction turns, followed by a final-answer turn. At each interaction turn t∈{0,…,T−1}t\in\{0,\dots,T-1\}, the model generates a thinking trace ItI_{t}, takes an action at∈𝒜a_{t}\in\mathcal{A}, and receives an observation ot∈𝒪o_{t}\in\mathcal{O} from the environment. The agent’s state is st=(Q,ℋt)s_{t}=(Q,\mathcal{H}_{t}), where ℋt=ℋ0:t\mathcal{H}_{t}=\mathcal{H}_{0:t} and ℋk:t=((Ik,ak,ok),…,(It−1,at−1,ot−1))\mathcal{H}_{k:t}=((I_{k},a_{k},o_{k}),\dots,(I_{t-1},a_{t-1},o_{t-1})) for k∈{0,…,t}k\in\{0,\dots,t\}, with ℋt:t\mathcal{H}_{t:t} denoting the empty history. For example, in a tool-use setting, the model takes an action by issuing a call to an external tool with appropriate parameters. At the final turn t=Tt=T, the model generates a thinking trace ITI_{T} and a final answer aTa_{T}, then terminates the interaction. The complete trajectory of T+1T+1 turns is 𝒯=((I0,a0,o0),…,(IT−1,aT−1,oT−1),(IT,aT))\mathcal{T}=((I_{0},a_{0},o_{0}),\dots,(I_{T-1},a_{T-1},o_{T-1}),(I_{T},a_{T})), which receives a binary reward R⁡(aT,Q)R(a_{T},Q), abbreviated as R∈{0,1}R\in\{0,1\}.

Multi-turn RL with GRPO. We use GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) to train the model in this multi-turn RL setting. At each training step, the rollout policy MθM_{\theta} generates GG trajectories {𝒯j}j=1G\{\mathcal{T}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{G} for the same query QQ through interactions with the environment, each receiving a reward RjR^{j}. Let A^j\widehat{A}^{\,j} denote the advantage for trajectory 𝒯j\mathcal{T}^{j}; its detailed formulation can be found in Appendix A.

Let 𝒯Mθj=((I0j,a0j),…,(ITjj,aTjj))\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}=((I^{j}_{0},a^{j}_{0}),\dots,(I^{j}_{T^{j}},a^{j}_{T^{j}})) denote the sequence of model-generated thinking traces and actions, including the final answer, in trajectory 𝒯j\mathcal{T}^{j}, where TjT^{j} is its number of interaction turns. We use |𝒯Mθj||\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}| to denote the total number of model-generated tokens in this sequence. The advantage A^j\widehat{A}^{\,j} is uniformly applied to every token in 𝒯Mθj\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}. Further details can be found in Appendix A.

Credit assignment. GRPO with only outcome rewards provides coarse credit for a multi-turn decision chain. As the advantage A^j\widehat{A}^{\,j} is broadcast uniformly to every model-generated token in the rollout, all turns share the same advantage. Such reward sparsity becomes more problematic for long-horizon agentic tasks as the trajectory length grows, because a single outcome reward must supervise more turns (Feng et al., 2025; Zhang, 2026). Providing better learning signals requires credit assignment, usually expressed through non-uniform advantage estimates. In this work, we focus on turn-level advantages A^tj\widehat{A}^{j}_{t}.

3 Methods

We present an approach that creates dense supervision signals from outcome rewards for long-horizon agentic RL using self-generated credit with intra-group rescaling via compaction. Our method, Self-Credit, combines three components: (1) the policy performs compaction by generating summaries of the interaction history, and the summaries cite important turns in the history as credit; (2) Intra-group rescaling refines this self-generated credit against the outcomes of other rollouts for the same prompt; (3) The rescaled credit is used to upweight the advantages of cited turns. Figure 2 illustrates Self-Credit.

3.1 Self-Compaction with Turn Citations

Compaction-augmented RL. Prior work introduces compaction into RLVR for long-horizon agentic tasks to address issues caused by growing context (Li et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026a; Lu et al., 2025). Compaction replaces the interaction history in the context with a shorter summary, allowing generation to continue conditioned on the query and summary.

During training, compaction is triggered whenever the context reaches or exceeds CC tokens at turn tt, where CC is a threshold chosen according to the effective context size of the LLM agent. When compaction is triggered, a summarizer MϕM_{\phi} produces a compact history ztz_{t} from the current interaction context:

ℋ~t′:t:={ℋt′:t,|(Q,ℋt′:t)|<C,zt,zt∼Mϕ(⋅∣Q,ℋt′:t),|(Q,ℋt′:t)|≥C.\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_{t^{\prime}:t}:=\begin{cases}\mathcal{H}_{t^{\prime}:t},&|(Q,\mathcal{H}_{t^{\prime}:t})|<C,\\ z_{t},\quad z_{t}\sim M_{\phi}(\cdot\mid Q,\mathcal{H}_{t^{\prime}:t}),&|(Q,\mathcal{H}_{t^{\prime}:t})|\geq C.\end{cases} (1)

Here, t′t^{\prime} is the most recent turn at which compaction was triggered before turn tt (t′=0t^{\prime}=0 if no compaction has been triggered yet), ℋt′:t\mathcal{H}_{t^{\prime}:t} is the context before compaction, and |(Q,ℋt′:t)||(Q,\mathcal{H}_{t^{\prime}:t})| denotes the context length. ℋ~t′:t\widetilde{\mathcal{H}}_{t^{\prime}:t} is the context after compaction: the previous interaction context is discarded and replaced by the summary; the model continues from the query and summary.

Compaction may be triggered multiple times as the context grows again after each summary. Let NjN^{j} be the number of context-replacing summaries generated in trajectory 𝒯j\mathcal{T}^{j}. The trajectory is then divided into Nj+1N^{j}+1 segments {𝒮ij}i=1Nj+1\{\mathcal{S}_{i}^{j}\}_{i=1}^{N^{j}+1}, each conditioned on the query and the preceding summary if exists.

Following compaction-augmented policy optimization methods such as SUPO (Lu et al., 2025), we extend the GRPO objective to:

𝒥SUM−RL​(θ)=𝔼⁡[1∑j=1G|𝒯Mθj|​∑j=1G∑i=1Nj+1∑ℓ=1|𝒮i,Mθj|min⁡(ρi,ℓj​A^j,clip⁡(ρi,ℓj,1−εlow,1+εhigh)​A^j)],\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{SUM-RL}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\Biggl[\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{G}|\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}|}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\sum_{i=1}^{N^{j}+1}\sum_{\ell=1}^{|\mathcal{S}^{j}_{i,M_{\theta}}|}\min\Bigl(\rho^{j}_{i,\ell}\widehat{A}^{\,j},\;\clip\bigl(\rho^{j}_{i,\ell},1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{low}},1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{high}}\bigr)\widehat{A}^{\,j}\Bigr)\Biggr], (2)

where 𝒮i,Mθj\mathcal{S}^{j}_{i,M_{\theta}} contains the trainable model-generated tokens of segment ii.

Here, 𝒯Mθj\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}} includes all trainable policy-generated tokens in the rollout, including summary tokens, so |𝒯Mθj|=∑i=1Nj+1|𝒮i,Mθj||\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}|=\sum_{i=1}^{N^{j}+1}|\mathcal{S}^{j}_{i,M_{\theta}}|. In other words, the objective computes one advantage per complete rollout trajectory and broadcasts it across the trainable tokens of all segments.

Summary with citations. Following Lu et al. (2025); Li et al. (2026b); Cursor Research et al. (2026), we use the policy model itself as the summarizer: Mϕ=MθM_{\phi}=M_{\theta}. During training and inference, when compaction is triggered, we prompt the policy model to summarize important information in the interaction history and cite important turns using their indices, producing a citation set K⊆{t′,…,t−1}K\subseteq\{t^{\prime},\dots,t-1\}. During training, the model is penalized for generating an invalid summary or citation to enforce the required format. We also prompt the model to provide citations at the end of the rollout to obtain signals for the final segment. Details of the prompt and required format can be found in Appendix B.1.

3.2 Intra-group Rescaling

However, relying solely on self-generated credit or rewards can reinforce undesired behaviors; related work shows that optimizing model-generated feedback can lead to hacking and instability (Shafayat et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025c; Wang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2026b). For example, instead of selectively citing important turns, the model can cite every turn in the context. Using such citations for credit assignment would then fail to provide selective learning signals.

To elicit better learning signals from self-generated citations, Self-Credit uses information already available in group-based RL without additional supervision or inference. For a given turn in a rollout, we examine similar turns across other rollouts in the same prompt group. A turn that appears more frequently across successful rollouts is more likely to be associated with success, and the same reasoning applies to failure. This provides within-group evidence for validating and refining the model’s self-generated credit.

Given a query QQ and its group of GG rollout trajectories {𝒯j}j=1G\{\mathcal{T}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{G}, let 𝒞\mathcal{C} and ℱ\mathcal{F} be the sets of successful and failed rollouts, respectively. Let BtjB_{t}^{j} denote the tt-th turn of trajectory 𝒯j\mathcal{T}^{j}. Following Feng et al. (2025), we assume that some turns appear more than once and can be matched across rollouts. For example, in search-agent tasks, two search actions can be matched if the sets of documents they retrieve have substantial overlap. In addition, we assume that different turns in a rollout contribute independently to the final outcome. Details of the matching procedure and a discussion of this assumption are provided in Appendix B.2.

Let n+​(Btj)n_{+}(B_{t}^{j}) and n−​(Btj)n_{-}(B_{t}^{j}) denote the numbers of successful and failed rollouts, respectively, in the group that cite a turn matching BtjB_{t}^{j}. Both numbers take the current rollout 𝒯j\mathcal{T}^{j} into consideration. We use these counts to distinguish the following three critical scenarios for a cited turn: (1) Repeated success: a matching turn is cited by at least τ+\tau_{+} successful rollouts and no failed rollouts; (2) Repeated failure: a matching turn is cited by at least τ−\tau_{-} failed rollouts and no successful rollouts; and (3) Mixed outcomes: a matching turn is cited by at least one successful rollout and at least one failed rollout.

Then, for a cited turn BtjB_{t}^{j} with A^j≠0\widehat{A}^{\,j}\neq 0, we assign a scaling weight as follows:

wtj:={wsA^j>0,n−(Btj)=0,and n+(Btj)≥τ+(Successes)1A^j>0​and ​n−​(Btj)>0(Mixed)βA^j>0,otherwise(Base credit)wfA^j<0,n+(Btj)=0,and n−(Btj)≥τ−(Failures)1A^j<0,otherwise.w_{t}^{j}:=\begin{cases}w_{s}&\widehat{A}^{\,j}>0,\ n_{-}(B_{t}^{j})=0,\ \text{and }n_{+}(B_{t}^{j})\geq\tau_{+}\quad\text{\footnotesize\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}(Successes)}\\[1.0pt] 1&\widehat{A}^{\,j}>0\ \text{and }n_{-}(B_{t}^{j})>0\quad\text{\footnotesize\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}(Mixed)}\\[2.0pt] \beta&\widehat{A}^{\,j}>0,\ \text{otherwise}\quad\text{\footnotesize\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}(Base credit)}\\[2.0pt] w_{f}&\widehat{A}^{\,j}<0,\ n_{+}(B_{t}^{j})=0,\ \text{and }n_{-}(B_{t}^{j})\geq\tau_{-}\quad\text{\footnotesize\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}(Failures)}\\[2.0pt] 1&\widehat{A}^{\,j}<0,\ \text{otherwise}.\\ \end{cases} (3)

In other words, we refine credit assignment in these three scenarios through intra-group comparisons: (1) Repeated success: we apply a larger scaling weight ws>βw_{s}>\beta to strengthen positive credit; (2) Repeated failure: we apply a scaling weight wf≥1w_{f}\geq 1 to strengthen the negative advantage; and (3) Mixed outcomes: we remove the β\beta upweighting for successful rollouts because the effect of the cited turn is uncertain. For all other cited turns, we retain the base weight of β\beta for positive advantages and 11 for negative advantages. For uncited turns t∉Kt\notin K, we do not change the advantages, so wtj=1w^{j}_{t}=1. The three scenarios are illustrated in Figure 2.

Intra-group rescaling is applied only to turns that can be matched across rollouts. Summary turns and final-answer turns are excluded from comparisons to preserve credit for summarization and answer commitment. Nonetheless, we show empirically in Section 6 that rescaling can still be triggered frequently, as most agentic actions within a group are similar when conditioned on the same query.

3.3 Advantage Reweighting

We leverage the rescaled weights for advantage reweighting. We use the citation set to replace the uniform advantage broadcast in Equation 2 with turn-level weights. For each model-generated token ℓ\ell in turn tt of trajectory 𝒯j\mathcal{T}^{j}, the token-level advantage is defined as follows:

A^t,ℓj:=A^j​wtj\widehat{A}^{j}_{t,\ell}:=\widehat{A}^{\,j}\,w^{\,j}_{t} (4)

In other words, all tokens in the same turn receive the same reweighted advantage using the assigned rescaled weight. In addition, in a successful rollout trajectory, summary turns and the final-answer turn are automatically treated as cited so that they receive credit without requiring explicit citations from the model.

3.4 Annealing the Weights

The importance of exploration and exploitation varies across different stages of LLM post-training (Cui et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2025). Since the rescaled weights can influence this balance, we design a learning curriculum with an annealing schedule for the repeated-failure penalty weight wfw_{f}. Stronger penalties early in training are intended to discourage repeatedly unsuccessful retrieval actions and stabilize search behaviors, while weaker penalties later allow more exploration.

4 Experimental Setup

4.1 Setup

Task

We evaluate our method on the following long-horizon multi-hop QA and deep research tasks: (1) BrowseComp-Plus (Chen et al., 2025b): LLM agents interact with a search engine and retrieve documents to solve multi-hop questions; (2) Deep research tasks: we evaluate on GAIA (Mialon et al., 2024) and xBench-DeepSearch (Chen et al., 2025a). These tasks include real-world questions requiring multi-step reasoning, web browsing, and tool use. For GAIA, we use its text-only subset.

Models

We train Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B (Yang et al., 2025), and Gemma4-E4B (Team et al., 2026) with thinking mode.

Training

For BrowseComp-Plus, we follow Xie et al. (2026) and split the dataset into 747 training examples for RL training and 83 test examples for evaluation. We use the BrowseComp-Plus static corpus and index as the search backend. For deep research tasks, we train on 1K deep research QA pairs from OpenResearcher (Li et al., 2026c) and use the OpenResearcher static browser as the tool use harness and search backend during training. For efficient training, we use a fully asynchronous rollout with VeRL (Sheng et al., 2024) and Megatron (Shoeybi et al., 2019) frameworks. For Self-Credit, we use τ+=τ−=2\tau_{+}=\tau_{-}=2 in all experiments. Details can be found under Appendix C.

4.2 Baselines

We compare against the following zero-shot and agentic RL baselines. The main differences between Self-Credit and these baselines can be found in Table 1. (1) Zero-shot evaluation of the base model does not use context management; (2) GRPO is applied to the multi-turn setting without any context management or turn-level credit assignment; (3) GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025) modifies group-based RL with turn-level credit assignment by re-grouping the same rollouts based on action states that are matched by repetitive actions. Turns sharing an identical environment observation are matched into groups, and within each group the action receives a standardized additive advantage adjustment; (4) SUPO (Lu et al., 2025) is a compaction-augmented RL baseline that implements a rolling summarization with a free-form summary and optimizes the uniform-credit objective. There is no citation instruction in the summarization prompt and no turn-level credit assignment; (5) ECHO (Xie et al., 2026) replaces free-form summarization in summarization-augmented RL with explicit turn selection: at each summarization, the policy emits a selection over its turn history, and the selected turn memories are carried into the next context in place of a summary. It routes token-level credit to the turns selected by the policy in successful rollouts.

4.3 Evaluation Protocol

For BrowseComp-Plus, we follow Chen et al. (2025b); Xie et al. (2026) and use the Qwen3-Embedding-8B (Zhang et al., 2025b) retriever and the BrowseComp-Plus static corpus index as the search engine during evaluation. We report LLM-as-a-judge accuracy, prompting a separate Qwen3-32B judge to determine whether the model-generated answer is semantically equivalent to the ground-truth answer. For deep research tasks, we follow Li et al. (2026c) to use open web search API instead of the static engine during evaluation. We report LLM-as-a-judge accuracy as well with the rubric from Gupta et al. (2026). For both tasks, we use temperature = 0.7 for decoding.

5 Results

Self-Credit outperforms strong RL baselines across settings. Table 3 reports test accuracy on BrowseComp-Plus. Self-Credit outperforms all baselines at both Qwen3 model scales and beats the strongest baseline by 5.65.6 points at 32B and 8.58.5 points at 8B. Table 3 summarizes results on deep research tasks by training a Gemma4-E4B model. On GAIA, Self-Credit achieves the highest accuracy and outperforms the strongest baseline by 4.94.9 points. On xBench-DeepSearch, Self-Credit outperforms the best baseline by 4.74.7 points. We also show that Self-Credit trains models that generalize better to OOD shorter horizon search QA datasets in Appendix D. These results demonstrate consistent gains across the evaluated model families and benchmarks with Self-Credit.

Self-Credit learns efficient long-horizon tool use. Training dynamics of different methods on BrowseComp-Plus shows the strength of Self-Credit from balancing depth and efficiency of tool use for long horizon tasks. Figure 3 shows later in training, Self-Credit typically uses fewer turns than ECHO does, while attaining high training reward. GRPO and GiGPO generate much shorter trajectories and exhibit lower training reward. This suggests that simply minimizing or maximizing interaction length for long-horizon tasks is insufficient (Yin et al., 2025). Together, these results show that Self-Credit supports sufficient exploration to gather useful evidence while limiting excessive interaction.

6 Analysis

6.1 Ablations

To isolate the importance of different components of Self-Credit, we conduct an ablation analysis with the following variants: (1) without intra-group rescaling: we train models to summarize with citations and upweight the advantages of all cited turns in rollouts with positive advantages; (2) without penalties for repeated failures; (3) without rescaling for mixed outcomes; (4) without self-generated citations: we apply intra-group rescaling and advantage reweighting to all turns instead of only the model-cited turns; (5) with random citations: we apply intra-group rescaling and advantage reweighting to a random set of turns in every segment, averaged over 3 seeds.

Table 4 summarizes the performance of these variants on BrowseComp-Plus. Among the intra-group components, rescaling repeated turns in failed rollouts is especially important for both model scales. Removing it reduces accuracy from 47.0%47.0\% to 34.9%34.9\% for Qwen3-32B and from 40.6%40.6\% to 26.5%26.5\% for Qwen3-8B. We observe that without penalties for repeated turns cited by failed rollouts, Qwen3-8B model learns to search excessively, likely caused by over-optimizing for the credit boost, and fails to learn to commit to an answer. Moreover, applying credit assignment to all turns or randomly selected turns reduces Qwen3-8B accuracy to 27.7%27.7\% and 32.5%32.5\%, respectively, showing that self-generated citations provide a better basis for credit assignment than using arbitrary turns.

Overall, these results show that the different components of Self-Credit work together: both self-generated citations and intra-group rescaling, especially over repeated failures, are important for achieving the best performance.

6.2 Quality of Credit Assignment

Self-Credit improves agentic tool use. We evaluate the quality of agentic tool use of models trained using different methods on BrowseComp-Plus, with a focus on two main types of tool use in this task: Search and Open. Details of the evaluation metrics are in Appendix E. Table 5 summarizes the results. Models trained with Self-Credit achieve higher Gold Searched, Gold Opened, and Answer Recall scores than the baselines at both model sizes.

Self-Credit generates better citations. To assess the quality of citations generated by different methods, we evaluate whether the cited turns perform actions that find gold documents for the agentic tasks. On BrowseComp-Plus, we use Open or Search actions that find gold documents as a proxy for critical actions, and we compute the F1 score of cited turns against the turns containing such actions. We also compute F1 against the important turn judged by Claude-4.6-Sonnet. Details of the evaluation metrics are in Appendix E. Table 6 reports the results for ECHO and Self-Credit; for reference, we introduce a random citation baseline that cites a subset of all turns in the rollout uniformly at random, and a baseline that cites all turns. Self-Credit achieves higher citation quality than ECHO and baselines for multiple metrics, especially better at identifying critical search turns. This indicates Self-Credit trains a better policy at finding the important turns in its generated rollouts, leading to a more reliable source for credit assignment.

Intra-group rescaling is applied selectively and accurately. We evaluate how frequently the intra-group rescaling is applied to cited turns during the early (0–60 steps) and late (60–115 steps) training stages on BrowseComp-Plus. We also report the precision of rescaling by checking whether it gives extra credit to actions that are related to the gold document, and reduces extra credit or give penalties for other less relevant actions. Details of the evaluation metrics are in Appendix E. Figure 4 shows that intra-group rescaling is triggered selectively. Compared with a random selection baseline, Self-Credit provides higher quality learning signals with high precision of crediting the good turns and downweighting or penalizing the other turns.

7 Related Work

Agentic RL for long-horizon tasks.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is widely used to post-train LLM agents (Jin et al., 2025; Singh et al., 2025; Qian et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025c), building on policy-gradient methods such as PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) and GRPO (Shao et al., 2024). In long-horizon tasks (Sun et al., 2026), growing interaction histories can exceed the context window, while sparse outcome rewards provide limited information about the contribution of individual actions (Wang and Ammanabrolu, 2025; Tang et al., 2026). Recent work addresses these challenges by using inference-time methods (Xu et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2026), incorporating context management systems (Li et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026a; Kang et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026) or self-compaction capability (Lu et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026b; Cursor Research et al., 2026) into the policy model through RL. Our work leverages self-compaction for context management during training for long horizon tasks.

Credit assignment under sparse outcome rewards.

Prior work derives finer grained credit given sparse outcome rewards from several sources, including learned critics (Zhou et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025d; Shi et al., 2026), process reward models (Zhang et al., 2026b; Zeng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026), hindsight information conditioned on answers (Tan et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b) and sampling (Choudhury, 2025; Zong et al., 2026), but these methods usually require additional rollouts or hindsight information not available in intermediate steps. Other methods reuse sampled rollouts to compare returns at similar states (Feng et al., 2025; He et al., 2026), or leverage confidence of the policy model (Wang et al., 2025a; Dong et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026a). Compared with prior work, our method combines signals that exist in standard group-based RL methods with self-compaction and rescales them using group-level statistics.

8 Conclusion

Training long-horizon LLM agents with RLVR is challenging because outcome rewards provide very sparse learning signals over long trajectories. We introduced Self-Credit, an end-to-end agentic RL method that creates dense supervision signals from a single sparse outcome reward through self-generated credit with intra-group rescaling. The policy model generates summaries with citations to critical turns during compaction, and these citations serve as self-generated credit. Self-Credit then refines this credit with intra-group rescaling, which compares cited actions across successful and failed rollouts for the same prompt, and uses the rescaled credit weights to selectively strengthen the advantages of tokens in model-cited turns. Self-Credit outperforms the strongest agentic RL baselines on challenging search QA and deep research tasks across models. These results suggest that self-generated signals can be utilized for effective credit assignment in long-horizon agentic RL.

Appendix A Formulation Details

A.1 GRPO Formulation

The advantage in GRPO is formulated as follows:

A^j=Rj−mean({Rj′}j′=1G)std({Rj′}j′=1G)+ϵ,j∈{1,…,G},\widehat{A}^{\,j}=\frac{R^{j}-\mean\big(\{R^{j^{\prime}}\}_{j^{\prime}=1}^{G}\big)}{\std\big(\{R^{j^{\prime}}\}_{j^{\prime}=1}^{G}\big)+\epsilon},\quad j\in\{1,\dots,G\}, (5)

where ϵ>0\epsilon>0 is a small constant for numerical stability.

The GRPO objective is defined as

𝒥GRPO(θ)=𝔼[1∑j=1G|𝒯Mθj|∑j=1G∑ℓ=1|𝒯Mθj|min(ρℓjA^j,clip(ρℓj,1−εlow,1+εhigh)A^j)],\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}\!\Biggl[\frac{1}{\sum_{j=1}^{G}|\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}|}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\sum_{\ell=1}^{|\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}|}\min\Bigl(\rho^{j}_{\ell}\widehat{A}^{\,j},\quad\clip\bigl(\rho^{j}_{\ell},1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{low}},1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{high}}\bigr)\widehat{A}^{\,j}\Bigr)\Biggr], (6)

where ρℓj\rho^{j}_{\ell} is the token-level importance ratio for the ℓ\ell-th token in 𝒯Mθj\mathcal{T}^{j}_{M_{\theta}}.

Importance sampling ratio in GRPO.

Importance sampling ratio is the ratio of its probability under MθM_{\theta} to that under MθoldM_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}, both conditioned on the context used to generate that token. Although token-level importance ratios and clipping can produce different gradient contributions, they do not provide turn-specific credit based on each action’s contribution to the outcome.

Appendix B Implementation Details

B.1 Prompts and Instructions

The summarization instruction used in our experiments is the following.

Citation format.

We introduce simple format gating on the generated citations: the citation line cannot be empty, and we strip out-of-range citations. An invalid citation line leads to a format error and makes the entire rollout receive a reward of 0.

Summary for the final segment.

Because compaction is only triggered at certain thresholds, turns in a short last segment might not get a chance to be cited, creating a systematic bias in the credit signal. Therefore, when a rollout trajectory is complete with a final answer, we force the model to generate an auxiliary summary of the final segment. This auxiliary summary is not a context-replacing summary and is not included in NjN^{j}.

B.2 Turn Matching

Matching turns across rollouts by actions.

Intra-group rescaling requires deciding when a cited turn in one rollout performs the same action as a turn in other rollouts for the same prompt. As defined in Section 2, a turn consists of thinking trace, an agentic action, and an observation from the environment. For the setting of long horizon agentic tasks, we focus on actions to match turns because LLM agents learn to perform the right actions during training. In the two settings below, instead of comparing the text of tool calls, which rarely repeats verbatim across rollouts, we identify each action by the evidence it retrieves from the environment.

BrowseComp-Plus.

On BrowseComp-Plus, the agent interacts with a fixed document corpus through three tools: (1) Search takes a natural-language query and returns a ranked list of retrieved documents, each of which has a document identifier (docid); (2) open_page takes a docid and returns the full text of that document; (3) finish submits the final answer and ends the interaction. We do not match turns with finish calls. For turns that leverage the other 2 types of tools, we use the following matching rules: (1) A search call is represented by the set of docids it returned. Within each prompt group, we match search turns by the overlap between the sets of retrieved docids. Two turns are matched if the Jaccard similarity of their sets of retrieved docids is at least 0.60.6; (2) For open_page, we match turns by the docid they opened , and two open_page turns match only if they opened the same document.

Deep research tasks.

For deep research tasks, the agent browses a fixed web corpus with OpenResearch harness during training through four tools: (1) search takes a natural-language query and returns the top 20 results as links; (2) open takes a link id or cursor from an earlier observation and returns the page content with line numbers; (3) find takes a text pattern and returns the lines in an opened page that match it; (4) finish submits the final answer and ends the interaction. Unlike on BrowseComp-Plus, the agent refers to pages through link ids (e.g., URLs) and cursors (location on the website) that are local to each rollout, making matching harder. Therefore, we identify each document by its docid in the OpenResearcher corpus, which the retriever returns as metadata hidden from the agent, instead of by links or cursors. As in BrowseComp-Plus, we do not match turns with finish calls, and we match search turns by the Jaccard similarity of their retrieved docids (at least 0.60.6) and open turns by the docid they opened. For find, two turns match if they found adjacent lines in the same document.

Turn matching for other tasks.

The matching rules above are instances of a general recipe: a task-specific function matches turns by the observations from those turns. Intra-group rescaling only needs these matches, so it can be applied unchanged to other agentic tasks once such a function is defined. This recipe is related to anchor-state grouping in GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025), which groups steps across trajectories that start from the same environment state, using exact matching or a similarity threshold over the state text. The difference lies in what is matched: GiGPO compares the states in which actions are taken, while Self-Credit compares the observations that cited actions obtain, which remains informative in open-ended environments where states rarely repeat. For example, in embodied tasks such as ALFWorld (Shridhar et al., 2021), a turn can be described by the object and receptacle it acts on (e.g., an object picked by the agent), together with whether the action succeeded.

Independence Assumption

In this work, we assume that different turns in a rollout contribute independently to the outcome, which is an approximation: an open action depends on the search that surfaced the document, and a late turn may only succeed because of evidence gathered earlier. We adopt the approximation because it keeps the comparison to counts over rollouts rather than over trajectory prefixes, which would rarely match.

Appendix C Training Configurations

C.1 General Hyperparameters

Following Xie et al. (2026); Li et al. (2026c), we use the same training configuration on BrowseComp-Plus and deep research tasks for all training methods, including Self-Credit:

  • •

    Optimization. We use a learning rate of 1×10−61\times 10^{-6} with a constant schedule and asymmetric clipping with ϵlow=0.20\epsilon_{\text{low}}=0.20 and ϵhigh=0.28\epsilon_{\text{high}}=0.28. The loss is averaged over tokens, with no entropy bonus, no KL penalty in either the loss or the reward, and no critic.

  • •

    Batching. Each training step uses 256 trajectories, split into 8 optimizer updates. We use 1616 prompts per step and 1616 rollouts per prompt.

  • •

    Sequence lengths. The maximum prompt length is 4096 tokens and the maximum response length is 32768 tokens. The threshold for compaction is 16384 tokens.

  • •

    Rollouts. Rollouts are generated asynchronously in a multi-turn agent loop, with tool calls in the Hermes format. Tool responses are truncated to 16K characters. The maximum number of assistant turns is 100.

    For BrowseComp-Plus, we allow the model to use 5 parallel tool calls and train for 115 steps, following the settings used by Xie et al. (2026). For deep research tasks, we allow the model to use 1 parallel tool call. We train for 100 steps. All training runs are conducted on 8x8 NVIDIA B200 GPU.

C.2 Hyperparameters of Baselines

We use the official implementations of the baseline methods.

ECHO.

We set turn-selection top-k to 55 and keep 33 recent turns verbatim.

GiGPO.

We use discount γ=0.95\gamma=0.95. Turns are grouped by similarity of the raw observation texts, as implemented by the original GiGPO paper.

C.3 Hyperparameters of Self-Credit

For all models on both datasets, we set maximum number of summary rounds to 10, β=1.5\beta=1.5, ws=2.5w_{s}=2.5, and wf=1.5w_{f}=1.5, annealed to wf=1.0w_{f}=1.0 linearly.

Appendix D OOD Generalization

D.1 Out-of-distribution Generalization

To evaluate the out-of-distribution transfer of different methods to shorter horizon tasks after training on long horizon, we evaluate zero-shot transfer of the Qwen3-32B policies to four out-of-distribution search-augmented QA benchmarks, following prior work (Jin et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2026). As shown in Table 7, Self-Credit achieves the highest average accuracy, 46.6%46.6\%, compared with 45.4%45.4\% for GRPO, 44.5%44.5\% for ECHO, and 44.3%44.3\% for SUPO. This demonstrates that tool use behaviors learned with long horizon training with Self-Credit generalize to shorter tasks as well.

Appendix E Details of Analysis

Tool-use quality metrics.

BrowseComp-Plus annotates each question with gold documents, which contain the answer, and a larger set of evidence documents, which are needed to support it. Gold Searched and Gold Opened are the percentages of questions for which at least one gold document appeared in any search result or was opened, respectively. Answer Recall is the fraction of a question’s gold documents that the policy either retrieved or opened, averaged over questions, and Evidence Recall is the same quantity computed over evidence documents.

Citation quality metrics in Table 6.

(1) Opened and Searched. We measure whether the turns a model cites contain the evidence needed for the answer, using the gold documents that BrowseComp-Plus annotates in the dataset. An Open or Search turn is considered important if it opened a gold document (Opened) or if one of its search results was a gold document (Searched). We compute the F1 of the cited turns against these turns, excluding the final answer turn. (2) LLM Judge. A useful exploratory turn may not find any gold documents but still inform the model about what to do next. While these turns still provide learning signals, the metrics above might overlook such turns. Therefore, we use LLM Judge F1 to score model citations against turns that Claude Sonnet 4.6 labels as decisive or as finding new relevant information, which does not rely on gold annotations. We use the LLM-as-judge prompt from Xu et al. (2026).

Rule firing and precision in Figure 4.

We measure how often each intra-group rescaling rule scenario is applied during training and whether it is applied to the right turns. The firing rate is the fraction of cited turns on which a rule is applied. The firing precision checks fired turns against turns that find the gold documents, i.e., turns that either opened a gold document or if one of its search results was a gold document. For the repeated success scenario, the firing precision is the share of fired turns that find gold documents. For repeated failure and mixed outcome, its precision is the share of fired turns that do not find gold documents.
